title: Cottony cushion scale on fruit trees

Header: Cottony cushion scale on fruit trees

Prevention: Cottony cushion scale is an insect covered of white wax and can cause considerable damage to trees by extracting significant quantities of sap and covering leaves with honeydew.
Select seedlings for planting that are free from scale insects.
Prune annually to prevent trees from touching.
Otherwise scale can easily spread from tree to tree.
Clean equipment with water before using it in other parts of the field in order to wash off scales and minimise spread.
Conserve natural predators such as ladybirds and green lacewings by planting attractive flowering plants on the ridge or border of the orchard.
Also avoid the use of persistent and broad spectrum pesticides.
Monitoring: Monitor field weekly to check for the presence of scale.
Search for scale on tree trunk, branches, twigs and leaves, particularly along leaf veins.
Adults: orange-brown, females have a fluted white cottony egg sac attached to their bodies which can be 2-3 times as long as body length (combined length can be about 1 cm).
Young/crawlers: red body with black legs and antenna.
Settle on leaf veins and produce white cottony secretion.
Black sooty mould (a fungus) on leaves, twigs and fruit which grows on the honeydew excreted by the scale.
Defoliation and dieback of twigs and small branches.
Ants that are collecting the honeydew excreted by scale.
On those 5 trees, check 5 randomly selected green twigs, leaves per twig and 5 randomly selected fruit per tree.
Consider taking action if 5-10 % of the material checked is infested with scale.
Be careful not to confuse young scale with vedalia beetle ( Rodolia cardinalis ) larvae - a predator of scale.
The young scales have black legs and antennae, whereas the vedalia beetle larvae have red legs and no visible antennae.
Young scales eventually turn orange-brown but beetle larvae eventually turn grey before becoming a black and red adult.
Direct Control: Natural enemies work best as a control method.
Chemicals may not be effective because females and their eggs are protected by a cottony egg sac and they are hard to reach when they rest deep in the tree canopy.
If available, use the vedalia beetle, Rodolia cardinalis as biological control in arid and hot inland areas where insecticides are not over-used.

Check the material every week or two and stir it with a stick to prevent the build up of debris which ants can use to cross.

If natural enemies are absent, the infestation is intolerable and scale populations mainly consist of the young crawler stage, then spray with a narrow range horticultural oil (follow application instructions on the bottle).
This is less disruptive to natural enemies and bees than many other insecticides.
